Inject | src/routes/reports.js:16 | The `status` query parameter is joined into the SQL text as a string. An attacker can change the query and read any table. | Entry: any user with a valid session sends `GET /reports?status=...`. `src/server.js:33` puts the decoded query string into `req.query` with no validation. Path: `src/server.js:31-32` checks only that the session is valid. At `src/routes/reports.js:16` the value goes into `sql` with no escaping. At `src/db.js:8`, `db.prepare(sql)` compiles that text, and only the owner `?` is bound. Example value: `x' UNION SELECT s.token, u.name, s.user_id, s.expires_at FROM sessions s JOIN users u ON u.id = s.user_id --`. Effect: the response holds the session tokens of all users, so the attacker can log in as any account. The value `' OR 1=1 --` also returns the reports of all owners. Guard: bind `status` as a `?` parameter at `src/routes/reports.js:16`.

Cross | src/routes/reports.js:35 | The `file` query parameter goes into `path.join` with no check that the result stays in the user's export folder. The attacker can read any file that the process can read. | Entry: any user with a valid session sends `GET /reports/export?file=../../reports.db`. `URLSearchParams` decodes `%2F`, so encoded slashes also work. Path: `src/server.js:33` gives the raw value. At `src/routes/reports.js:35`, `path.join(EXPORTS, String(user.id), file)` resolves `..` segments to a path outside `EXPORTS/<id>`, and no prefix check follows. At `src/routes/reports.js:37-39`, `fs.createReadStream(file)` streams the file to the response. Effect: the attacker reads the export files of other users (`../<otherId>/x.csv`). The attacker also reads the SQLite database (default `reports.db` in the working directory, `src/db.js:3`, next to the default `exports` folder at `src/routes/reports.js:7`). That file holds every session token and every report. Any other file the process can read is open too. Guard: at `src/routes/reports.js:35`, resolve the path and refuse it unless it starts with `path.join(EXPORTS, String(user.id)) + path.sep`, or allow only a basename.

Access | src/routes/reports.js:61 | `DELETE /reports/:id` deletes by id only and does not check the owner. Any user can delete the reports of any other user. | Entry: any user with a valid session sends `DELETE /reports/<n>`. Report ids are sequential integers (`(\d+)`, line 59), so an attacker can guess them. Path: `src/server.js:31-32` checks only that a session exists. At `src/routes/reports.js:61`, `DELETE FROM reports WHERE id = ?` binds only `match[1]` and has no `AND owner = ?`. The other routes in the range do check the owner (lines 15, 26, 47), and so does the base's `DELETE /projects/:id` at `src/server.js:21`. Effect: the attacker can destroy the data of any user and can learn which ids exist from the 204/404 answer. Guard: add `AND owner = ?` with `user.id` at `src/routes/reports.js:61`.

count: 3

I also checked two other routes and found no hole by the lens's rules:
- **`/reports/search`:** the user's pattern goes into `RegExp`. That is a slowness risk (ReDoS), which the lens excludes.
- **`/reports/:id/cover`:** the owner check is at line 47. The `convert` arguments come from a numeric id and from `REPORT_FONT`, which only the deployment sets. `execFile` uses no shell.
